course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 4
firstTopic.summary: The context for Period 4: a more participatory democracy and a new national culture, an economy transformed by innovation, and a nation that expanded westward and argued over slavery, 1800–1848.

topic.title: The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson
topic.summary: How the election of 1800, Jefferson's presidency, the Supreme Court's early decisions, and the Louisiana Purchase shaped national politics and the nation's reach across North America.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: The presidential election of 1800 is significant mainly because
choices: the Supreme Court decided the winner after the Electoral College result ended in a tie
Federalist leaders refused to leave office until the Twelfth Amendment forced them out
power passed from one party to another peacefully after a bitterly contested election
Jefferson and Adams agreed to share the presidency for two terms to end the dispute
questions.explanation: Jefferson's election showed that the republic could transfer power from the Federalists to the Democratic-Republicans without violence.
choiceExplanations: The House of Representatives, not the Court, chose the president.
The Federalists accepted the result, and the Amendment came later.
Jefferson's election showed that the republic could transfer power from the Federalists to the Democratic-Republicans without violence.
The presidency was never shared.
questions.distinguisher: The Supreme Court choice is close because the Court later became powerful, but the House of Representatives decided the 1800 tie.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The Embargo Act of 1807 was intended to
choices: pressure Britain and France to respect American neutral rights by cutting off trade
protect American manufacturers from foreign competition by raising tariffs on British goods
punish Native nations that had allied with Britain along the northwestern frontier
raise money for the army by placing a new tax on goods exported from American ports
questions.explanation: Jefferson hoped that the loss of American trade would force Britain and France to stop seizing American ships, but the embargo hurt American merchants and was repealed in 1809.
choiceExplanations: Jefferson hoped that the loss of American trade would force Britain and France to stop seizing American ships, but the embargo hurt American merchants and was repealed in 1809.
The embargo stopped trade; it was not a tariff to shelter manufacturers.
The embargo concerned trade with Europe.
The embargo ended exports and did not tax them.
questions.distinguisher: The tariff choice is close because the embargo changed trade, but it halted exports and imports instead of raising duties.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), the Supreme Court
choices: ordered the secretary of state to deliver the commissions of the appointed Federalist judges
ruled that states could not tax the national bank chartered by Congress
gave Congress the power to regulate trade among the states and with other nations
asserted its power to decide whether acts of Congress violate the Constitution
questions.explanation: Chief Justice Marshall's opinion established judicial review, the Court's power to judge the constitutionality of laws.
choiceExplanations: The Court said it could not issue that order.
That was the ruling in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
That was the ruling in Gibbons v. Ogden (1824).
Chief Justice Marshall's opinion established judicial review, the Court's power to judge the constitutionality of laws.
questions.distinguisher: The commissions choice is close because the case began as a dispute over commissions, but the Court's lasting ruling concerned judicial review.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The Supreme Court's decision in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) established that
choices: the Constitution barred Congress from creating a national bank without the consent of the states
federal law was supreme over state law and Congress could charter a national bank
states could tax federal institutions that operated inside their borders if they chose
the Court lacked the power to review the actions of state governments under the Constitution
questions.explanation: The Court held that the Constitution's implied powers allowed the bank and that a state could not tax a federal institution.
choiceExplanations: The Court upheld the bank and the power of Congress.
The Court held that the Constitution's implied powers allowed the bank and that a state could not tax a federal institution.
The Court ruled that Maryland could not tax the national bank.
The decision asserted federal supremacy over the states.
questions.distinguisher: The state tax choice is close because the case began with a state tax, but the Court ruled against the state.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Jefferson agreed to buy the Louisiana Territory in 1803?
choices: Control of New Orleans and the Mississippi River was vital to western farmers and trade
He believed that the Constitution clearly gave the president the power to purchase territory
France had threatened to attack the United States unless it bought the territory
Spain had asked the United States to take over its colonies in the American West
questions.explanation: Western farmers depended on the Mississippi and New Orleans, so Jefferson set aside his doubts about the Constitution to secure the region.
choiceExplanations: Western farmers depended on the Mississippi and New Orleans, so Jefferson set aside his doubts about the Constitution to secure the region.
Jefferson was unsure whether the Constitution allowed it.
France offered the land in order to raise money for its European wars.
Spain had given Louisiana to France, which sold it.
questions.distinguisher: The Constitution choice is close because Jefferson wanted to follow it closely, but he was unsure that the document allowed the purchase.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Jefferson sent the Lewis and Clark expedition (1804–1806) to
choices: establish farming settlements along the Columbia River for American families
negotiate a treaty with France that would fix the western border of the purchase
explore the Louisiana Territory and the route to the Pacific and to gather information
locate gold deposits that could pay the national debt that the purchase had created
questions.explanation: Lewis and Clark mapped routes, gathered information about land and peoples, and strengthened American claims in the Northwest.
choiceExplanations: The expedition explored and did not establish settlements.
The treaty with France had been signed in 1803.
Lewis and Clark mapped routes, gathered information about land and peoples, and strengthened American claims in the Northwest.
The expedition's goals were exploration, trade, and science.
questions.distinguisher: The settlements choice is close because the expedition built winter camps, but its purpose was to explore and not to settle.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a continuity in American politics from the 1790s into the early 1800s?
choices: Both parties agreed that the tariff should rise and that the national bank should be ended
The two national parties continued to disagree over federal power and relations with Europe
Presidential elections stopped being contested after the Twelfth Amendment took effect in 1804
Both parties favored joining Britain in a war against France to protect American trade
questions.explanation: The parties that formed in the 1790s over federal power and the French Revolution continued to debate those matters in the early 1800s.
choiceExplanations: The parties disagreed on the powers of the federal government.
The parties that formed in the 1790s over federal power and the French Revolution continued to debate those matters in the early 1800s.
Elections remained competitive.
The parties disagreed about Britain and France, and the nation stayed neutral.
questions.distinguisher: The Twelfth Amendment choice is close because it changed the electoral system in 1804, but elections remained contested.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The Supreme Court's early claims to review laws are best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: The Articles of Confederation, which had set up a national judiciary with power over the states
A Federalist plan to remove Jefferson from the presidency by order of the courts
A constitutional rule that required the Court to approve each bill before Congress could vote
The new nation's effort to define the Constitution and the balance of power among the branches
questions.explanation: Americans were still working out what the Constitution meant, and the Marshall Court claimed the final say on those questions.
choiceExplanations: The Articles created no national courts.
The Federalists did not seek to remove Jefferson by court order.
The Constitution gives the Court no such role in the lawmaking process.
Americans were still working out what the Constitution meant, and the Marshall Court claimed the final say on those questions.
questions.distinguisher: The Federalist plan choice is close because the case arose from Federalist appointments, but it did not involve removing the president.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Jefferson's statement that “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists” was most likely intended to
choices: persuade Federalist leaders to give up their party and join the Democratic-Republicans
announce that Congress had outlawed political parties as a danger to the republic
lessen the bitterness between the parties after a hard-fought election
defend the Alien and Sedition Acts that the Federalists had passed in 1798
questions.explanation: Jefferson spoke to a divided nation and stressed principles that both parties shared in order to calm party feeling.
choiceExplanations: He spoke of shared principles, not of ending the Federalist Party.
Parties were not outlawed.
Jefferson spoke to a divided nation and stressed principles that both parties shared in order to calm party feeling.
Jefferson and his party had opposed those Acts.
questions.distinguisher: The join-the-party choice is close because Jefferson hoped to win over moderates, but his address stressed shared principles and did not demand a change of party.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Thomas Jefferson, delivering his First Inaugural Address on March 4, 1801, after the contested election of 1800 in which he defeated the incumbent, John Adams
stimulusBlocks.citation: Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address (March 4, 1801). NLTK inaugural corpus, 1801-Jefferson.txt.
stimulusBlocks.note: Jefferson uses “Republicans” and “Federalists” as the names of the two parties and also as words for principles that he says all Americans share: republican government and a federal union.
stimulusBlocks.text:
But every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle. We have called by different names brethren of the same principle. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.

Equal and exact justice to all men, of whatever state or persuasion, religious or political; peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none; the support of the State governments in all their rights, as the most competent administrations for our domestic concerns and the surest bulwarks against antirepublican tendencies; . . . .

questions.subskillText: Identify a source’s point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience.

questions.prompt: Which of the following positions is best supported by Jefferson's list of principles in the second paragraph?
choices: Support for a strong central government and a permanent alliance with Britain
Support for the rights of the state governments and avoidance of alliances with other nations
Support for an end to commerce with foreign nations in order to protect the states
Support for federal control of domestic concerns and a national religion
questions.explanation: Jefferson calls for “the support of the State governments in all their rights” and “entangling alliances with none.”
choiceExplanations: He praised state governments and rejected alliances.
Jefferson calls for “the support of the State governments in all their rights” and “entangling alliances with none.”
He supported commerce and friendship with all nations.
He supported equal justice regardless of religious persuasion and the states' role in domestic matters.
questions.distinguisher: The strong central government choice is close because it describes the Federalist position, which Jefferson did not state in the excerpt.

questions.prompt: The phrase “entangling alliances with none” is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: The Monroe Doctrine's warning against European intervention in the Western Hemisphere
The Treaty of Alliance with France that Congress had approved during the Revolution
A plan to join the Holy Alliance of European monarchies in order to protect trade
Earlier American efforts to stay neutral in the wars between Britain and France
questions.explanation: Leaders from Washington on warned against permanent alliances, and neutrality shaped policy during the wars of the French Revolution.
choiceExplanations: The Monroe Doctrine came in 1823, after this speech.
That alliance was the kind of entanglement leaders now wished to avoid.
The Holy Alliance formed in 1815, and the United States did not join it.
Leaders from Washington on warned against permanent alliances, and neutrality shaped policy during the wars of the French Revolution.
questions.distinguisher: The Monroe Doctrine choice is close because both statements concern foreign policy, but the Doctrine was announced more than twenty years later.
